newsitem.title: UK: Labour twists knife in UK Conservative wounds.
newsitem.headline: Labour twists knife in UK Conservative wounds.

text.p: The Labour government added spice on Monday to the bitter battle to lead Britain's shattered Conservative party by claiming it was in contact with several Conservative members of parliament dismayed by their party's anti-European drift.

A senior government official said unease in the ranks of Conservative pro-Europeans had grown since William Hague, favourite in the three-man leadership race, hardened his stance against the European Union's planned single currency.

"It is true to say we have a number of informal links with Conservative MPs and we intend to maintain those links," the official said. Conservative MPs hold the second round of their leadership ballot on Tuesday.

He said the discussions had centred on how pro-European Conservatives could "relate" to the Labour government if the new Conservative leader were to rule out membership of economic and monetary union (EMU) once and for all.

The official said pro-European Conservatives, who are backing ex-finance minister Kenneth Clarke in the ballot, were alarmed not just by Euro-sceptic challenger John Redwood, a former Welsh secretary.
He said some were also "pretty horrified" by Hague, who came out explicitly last week against joining the single currency.

Although Conservatives dismissed the government official's disclosure as mischief-making, it followed warnings by two of the party's most senior figures that electing a leader on a right-wing anti-European platform could further alienate voters.
Former deputy prime minister Lord Geoffrey Howe said on Monday that voters had signalled by electing Labour on May 1 that they wanted a more balanced view of Europe.

"What I'm more concerned about is that if we're led either by William Hague or John Redwood, there will open up an even wider gap between the Conservative party and the great mass of public opinion, business opinion..." Howe said.

By focusing obsessively on the single currency, the Conservatives risked repeating the mistake of the Labour party of the early 1980s, which made itself unelectable by indulging in a purely doctrinal debate over nuclear disarmament, he said.
"The Tory party risks drifting away from the people.

"If it is to get back in touch with the people whose votes we need, then we need to return to the centre ground and that is surely the cataclysmic lesson of the election we've just lost so catastrophically," Howe said.

Clarke himself cautioned that the Conservatives could head into an ideological ghetto under Redwood or Hague, saying few pro-Europeans would be willing to serve under them if they based their appeal on hard-line Euro-scepticism.
An unrepentant Redwood said the Conservatives, who are left with just 164 MPs in the 659-seat House of Commons, could rebuild their fortunes only if they rediscovered their beliefs.

"You will not unite the Conservative party with more fudge. You can with a new hard centre of unshakeable principle and common sense policy. I don't want to split the difference. I want to make the difference. That is what I offer," he said.
To win the second round of the ballot, a candidate needs the votes of more than half the ConservatiMps. If there is no winner, the two front-runners slug it out on Thursday.
